{{Short description|American mathematician (1899–1980)}}
'''Frank Vigor Morley''' (4 January 1899 – 8 October 1980) was an American mathematician, author, editor and publishing executive. As had his two older brothers, [[Christopher Morley|Christopher]] and [[Felix Morley|Felix]], Morley attended [[Haverford College]] and then studied at the [[University of Oxford]] as a [[Rhodes Scholar]].  Morley worked in book publishing in London and New York and played a significant role in the early history of the publishing firm [[Faber and Faber]], where he became a close friend of the poet [[T. S. Eliot]].

==Life==
Morley was born on 4 January 1899 in [[Haverford, Pennsylvania]]<ref>Biographical Catalog of the Matriculates of Haverford College... 1833 - 1922 (Philadelphia, Pa.: The Alumni Association, 1922), p. 693.</ref> where his father [[Frank Morley]] was Professor of Mathematics at [[Haverford College]].  In 1900 his father was named chairman of the mathematics department at [[Johns Hopkins University]] and the family removed to [[Baltimore, Maryland]].<ref>obituary "Frank V. Morley, Author and Retired Publishing Executive," ''The Baltimore Sun'' 9 October 1980, p. 10</ref> As had his two, older brothers, [[Christopher Morley|Christopher]] and [[Felix Morley|Felix]], Frank returned to Haverford College for his undergraduate education which, however, was interrupted in 1917 when Morley left school to serve as 2nd lieutenant in an Engineering unit based at [[Hog Island, Philadelphia]], during World War I.<ref>Biographical Catalog of the Matriculates of Haverford College... 1833 - 1922 (Philadelphia, Pa.: The Alumni Association, 1922), p. 693.</ref><ref>obituary "Frank V. Morley, Author and Retired Publishing Executive," ''The Baltimore Sun'' 9 October 1980, p. 10</ref>
  
Morley received his [[bachelor's degree]] in 1918 from Johns Hopkins University.<ref>Biographical Catalog of the Matriculates of Haverford College... 1833 - 1922 (Philadelphia, Pa.: The Alumni Association, 1922), p. 693.</ref><ref>obituary "Frank V. Morley, Author and Retired Publishing Executive," ''The Baltimore Sun'' 9 October 1980, p. 10</ref>  Morley won a [[Rhodes Scholarship]], as did his two brothers, and attended [[New College, Oxford]]; they were the only family of three brothers to receive this prestigious scholarship.<ref>Helen McK. Oakley, ''Three Hours for Lunch: The Life and Time of Christopher Morley'' (Searingtown, New York: Watermill Publishers, 1976), p. 27.</ref> Morley earned a doctorate in mathematics from Oxford in 1923.<ref>"[https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.bams/1183500344 Frank Morley -- In Memoriam]" ''American Mathematical Society Bulletin'' ( March 1938) p. 167.  Accessed 18 October 2020</ref>   Morley remained in England, working at ''[[The Times Literary Supplement]]'', and then as London manager for the publishers of ''[[The Century Magazine]].''<ref>''The Letters of T. S. Eliot: Volume 5: 1930-1931'' (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 2011), p. 87</ref>  [[Geoffrey Faber]] hired Morley in 1929 to be co-director of the newly re-organized publishing firm [[Faber and Faber]].<ref>Jonathan Galassi, "The Unlikely History of Faber & Faber," in ''The New Yorker'', 23 July 2019 https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/the-unlikely-history-of-faber-and-faber Accessed 18 October 2020.</ref>  In this capacity Morley worked with and became close friends with [[T. S. Eliot]], then an editor at Faber and Faber.  Morley assisted Eliot in quickly finding new accommodation when Eliot separated from his wife.<ref>''The Letters of T.S. Eliot: Volume 5: 1930-1931'' (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 2011), p. 87</ref>  Eliot wrote the  poem "Cows" for Morley's children.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Morley | first = Frank | date = Winter 1966 | issue = 1 | journal = The Sewanee Review | jstor = 27541387 | pages = 110–133 | title = A few recollections of Eliot | volume = 74}} Cf. 133.</ref>

In 1933 Morley and his father [[Frank Morley]] published the "stimulating volume," ''Inversive Geometry''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Snyder, Virgil|author-link=Virgil Snyder|title=Review: Frank Morley and F. V. Morley, ''Inversive Geometry''|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1934|volume=40|issue=5|pages=374–375|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183497418|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1934-05848-8|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>[[Henry Forder]] (1934) Review:''Inversive Geometry'', [[The Mathematical Gazette]] 18:127–9</ref> The book develops [[complex number]]s as a tool for geometry and [[Complex analysis|function theory]].

In 1936 Morley's novel ''War Paint'' was published. Reviewing the book in ''[[The New English Weekly]]'', [[George Orwell]] described it as "an exceedingly naïve adventure story, and at the same time a sort of [[Chelsea Hospital]] for superannuated jokes."<ref>{{cite book|first=George|last=Orwell|author-link=George Orwell|chapter=Review|orig-year=1936|page=185|title=The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters of George Orwell, Volume 1: An Age Like This 1920–1940|editor1-first=Sonia|editor1-last=Orwell|editor1-link=Sonia Orwell|editor2-first=Ian|editor2-last=Angus|editor2-link=Ian Angus (librarian)|publisher=Penguin|year=1968}}</ref>

In 1939 Morley left London for New York to become Vice-President, and Director of the Trade Editorial Department at [[Harcourt (publisher)|Harcourt, Brace, Jovanovich]].<ref>Helen McK. Oakley, ''Three Hours for Lunch: The Life and Time of Christopher Morley'' (Searingtown, New York: Watermill Publishers, 1976), p. 293.</ref>  Shortly thereafter Harcourt published 
''My Sister and I'' by Dirk van der Heide (1941), the story of the German [[German bombing of Rotterdam in World War II|bombing of Rotterdam]] ostensibly written by an 11-year-old refugee to England and thence to the United States. ''My Sister and I'' enjoyed considerable commercial and critical success, but in the 1980s was discovered to have been a literary fabrication conducted by Harcourt, under Morley's supervision, to encourage American participation in [[World War II]], possibly with guidance or encouragement from British intelligence services.<ref>Sheldon Winkler, "My Sister and I: the True Story" in  ''The Music of World War II: War Songs and Their Stories'' (Hoosick Falls, New York: Merriam Press, 2019) pp. 21-28.</ref> During the war, Morley also served on the [[National War Labor Board (1942-1945)|National War Labor Board]].<ref>''The Letters of T.S. Eliot: Volume 5: 1930-1931'' (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 2011), p. 87</ref>  Following the war, Morley returned to England to become Director of the publisher [[Eyre & Spottiswoode]] from which he ultimately retired.<ref>''The Letters of T.S. Eliot: Volume 5: 1930-1931'' (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 2011), p. 87</ref><ref>obituary "Frank V. Morley, Author and Retired Publishing Executive," ''The Baltimore Sun'' 9 October 1980, p. 10</ref>

==Literary connections==
As an editor and publisher, Morley enjoyed a wide correspondence and friendships with many prominent authors and literary figures of the day.  These included Eliot, [[Ezra Pound]], [[Lewis Mumford]], and [[Walter De la Mare]], as well as Morley's eldest brother [[Christopher Morley|Christopher]], who was a notable author and powerful promoter of literature.  It was Frank Morley who suggested to Pound in 1933 that he write an autobiography, which resulted in Pound's 1938 work ''[[Guide to Kulchur]]''.<ref>"Anderson Araujo, "Introduction" in ''A Companion to Ezra Pound's Guide to Kulcher: Guide to Kulcher'' (pp. 1-18). Liverpool University Press, 2018.  https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/companion-to-ezra-pounds-guide-to-kulcher/introduction/C46EC8FD4CEC7499E8685CA0F770D97B  Accessed 18 October 2020</ref>  Morley's literary correspondence is now held chiefly by the [[New York Public Library]]'s [[Berg Collection]].<ref>[http://archives.nypl.org/brg/19320 Finding Aid and Description of the F.V. Morley Collection, New York Public Library] Accessed 18 October 2020</ref>

With his brother Christopher, Morley had long been an admirer of the [[Sherlock Holmes]] stories by [[Sir Arthur Conan Doyle]]. Christopher originated [[The Baker Street Irregulars]] in 1934 as an informal meeting of his friends and others interested in Holmes, but in order to restrict membership to those who were truly knowledgeable if not expert in the stories, and eliminate mere casual readers of Conan Doyle, a membership test in the form of a crossword puzzle was devised by Frank V. Morley. This was published in Christopher's "Bowling Green" column in the May 1934 issue of the ''[[Saturday Review of Literature]]''.<ref>Helen McK. Oakley, ''Three Hours for Lunch: The Life and Time of Christopher Morley'' (Searingtown, New York: Watermill Publishers, 1976), pp. 224-232.</ref>
   
Morley traveled widely throughout England before and after the Second World War, incorporating his reading and observations into a number of non-fiction works of literary history and tourism, the last of which, ''Literary Britain'', was published only days before his death on 8 October 1980 at age 82 in [[Buckinghamshire]], England.<ref>obituary "Frank V. Morley, Author and Retired Publishing Executive," ''The Baltimore Sun'' 9 October 1980, p. 10</ref>

==Personal life==
Morley married Christina McLeod Innes 14 May 1925.  They had two sons and two daughters: Donald, Oliver, Peregrine, and Susannah.<ref>obituary "Frank V. Morley, Author and Retired Publishing Executive," ''The Baltimore Sun'' 9 October 1980, p. 10</ref>

* ''[https://hdl.handle.net/2027/wu.89096955117 Travels in East Anglia] Travels in East Anglia]'' (New York: Harcourt, [1923]) now available from [[HathiTrust]]

* ''Whaling North and South'' with J.S. Hodgson (New York: Century, 1926) 
* ''East South East'' (London: Longmans, 1929)
* ''Lamb before Elia'' (London: J. Cape, 1932)
* ''[https://hdl.handle.net/2027/uc1.b4074019 Inversive Geometry]'' (with father Frank Morley), (New York: Ginn & Co., 1933) now available from [[HathiTrust]]
* ''War Paint, a Story of Adventure''  (London: Faber & Faber, 1936) published in the United States as ''The Wreck of the Active'' (Boston and New York, Houghton Mifflin Company, 1936)
* ''[https://hdl.handle.net/2027/uc1.$b281525 My One Contribution to Chess]'' (New York: B.W. Huebsch, 1945) now available from [[HathiTrust]]
* ''Death in Dwelly Lane'' (London: Eyre & Spottiswoode, 1952)
* ''The Great North Road: A Journey in History'' (New York: Macmillan, 1961) 
*  “A Few Recollections of Eliot.” ''The Sewanee Review'', vol. 74, no. 1, 1966, pp.&nbsp;110–133. now available from [http://www.jstor.org/stable/27541387 JSTOR] Accessed 18 Oct. 2020.
* ''The Long Road West: A Journey in History'' (London: Chatto & Windus, New York: Dial Press, 1971)
* ''Literary Britain: A Reader's Guide to Its Writers and Landmarks''  (New York: Harper & Row, 1980)
